docs.title: Apollo Reads
docs.text:
Free read-along stories for kids, any time a grown-up is busy.

Press play, turn on captions, and read together. Every book page has tips for parents, questions to talk about, and links to borrow the book free from your library.

📚 Browse the Library 💛 Parents' Corner

docs.title: About
docs.text:
Apollo's Epiphany

One night, not so long ago, in a California town not so far away, while we were reading bedtime stories, my son Apollo stopped us and asked if all childrens' parents read them bedtime stories.

After I explained to Apollo that not all parents had the time, money, or ability to read to their children every night, Apollo demanded that we read to all of those children. Apollo recently turned 5, and he has been learning to read, so he wanted to be the narrator on all of these stories! Unfortunatley, his current reading level won't quite cut it for bedtime stories. BUT someday I know Apollo will transition into my current role, and he will become the ApolloReads.com narrator!

We are doing this entirely voluntarily to satisfy Apollo's emotionally intelligent demand that we bring reading and bedtime stories to all the children on the internet whose parents can't. Please join me in thanking Apollo for his kind heart at such a young age, and we both hope you enjoy our bedtime stories.

-- Dad

by Tracey West

🌱 Early Readers 🌻 Growing Readers 📚 Chapter Book⏱ 46 min read-along Ages6–9 (suggested)Reading levelK–2Pages96Published2020PublisherDragon MastersISBN9781338540260 ⭐ We read this!▶ Watch on YouTube

docs.title: 📖 About the Book
docs.text: The dark wizard Maldred has trapped dragon master Eko as well as wizards who have opposed him, all of them frozen in time and space inside a wall in his hideout; so Drake and Worm set out to seek the help of the Time Dragon--but when a imp named Beezel interferes Drake ends up back in his own past, and he must find a way to get back to the present.

docs.title: 🧠 Read Together
docs.text:
Tips for 🌱 Early Readers (ages 5–7). Reading together for just 15 minutes a day builds vocabulary, focus and a lifelong love of stories.

Before watchingWhile watchingAfter watchingTalk about it
  • Turn on captions (CC). Reading along with spoken words is one of the best ways to build fluency.
  • Read the title out loud together and talk about what you expect.
  • Pause the video and let your child read the next line before the narrator does.
  • Point out sight words (the, and, said, was) each time they appear.
  • Ask: “Who was the main character? What problem did they have? How was it solved?”
  • Have your child read one page aloud to you — or to a pet or stuffed animal audience!
  • Who was your favorite character in Dragon Masters, and why?
  • What was the problem in the story? How did it get solved?
  • If you could change the ending, what would happen instead?
  • How do you think the main character felt at the end?

🧸 Picture Book Pals 🌱 Early Readers 📚 Picture Book⏱ 18 min read-along Ages3–7 (suggested)Reading levelPre-KPages44Published2001PublisherFondo de Cultura EconómicaISBN9780008124489 ⭐ We read this!▶ Watch on YouTube

docs.title: ▶️ Watch & Read Along

docs.title: 📖 About the Book
docs.text: Having soothed the hurt feelings of one group who threatened to quit, Duncan now faces a whole new group of crayons asking to be rescued. From Maroon Crayon, who was lost beneath the sofa cushions and then broken in two after Dad sat on him; to poor Turquoise, whose head is now stuck to one of Duncan's stinky socks after they both ended up in the dryer together; to Pea Green, who knows darn well that no kid likes peas and who ran away—each and every crayon has a woeful tale to tell and a plea to be brought home to the crayon box.

docs.title: 🧠 Read Together
docs.text:
Tips for 🧸 Picture Book Pals (ages 3–5). Reading together for just 15 minutes a day builds vocabulary, focus and a lifelong love of stories.

Before watchingWhile watchingAfter watchingTalk about it
  • Look at the cover together and ask: “What do you think this story is about?”
  • Turn on captions (CC) so your child sees the words while hearing them.
  • Pause and ask “What do you think will happen next?” There are no wrong answers!
  • Hunt for letters: can your child spot the first letter of their name on screen?
  • Ask your child to retell the story in three parts: beginning, middle, end.
  • Draw a favorite picture from the story and label it together.
  • Can you find your favorite picture?
  • What sounds did you hear in the story?
  • What colors did you see?

docs.title: Because of Winn-Dixie
docs.text:
by Kate DiCamillo

🚀 Chapter Champions 📚 Chapter Book⏱ 2 hr 26 min read-along Ages10–12Reading levelGrades 4–7Pages182Published2000PublisherTaiwan dong fang chu ban sheISBN9780758765123 ⭐ We read this!▶ Watch on YouTube

docs.title: ▶️ Watch & Read Along
docs.text: Tap to play

docs.title: 📖 About the Book
docs.text:
Ten-year-old India Opal Buloni describes her first summer in the town of Naomi, Florida, and all the good things that happen to her becauThe summer Opal and her father, the preacher, move to Naomi, Florida, Opal goes into the Winn-Dixie supermarket—and comes out with a dog. A big, ugly, suffering dog with a sterling sense of humor. A dog she dubs Winn-Dixie. Because of Winn-Dixie, the preacher tells Opal ten things about her absent mother, one for each year Opal has been alive. Winn-Dixie is better at making friends than anyone Opal has ever known, and together they meet the local librarian, Miss Franny Block, who once fought off a bear with a copy of WAR AND PEACE. They meet Gloria Dump, who is nearly blind but sees with her heart, and Otis, an ex-con who sets the animals in his pet shop loose after hours, then lulls them with his guitar.

Opal spends all that sweet summer collecting stories about her new friends and thinking about her mother. But because of Winn-Dixie or perhaps because she has grown, Opal learns to let go, just a littlse of her big ugly dog Winn-Dixie.

docs.title: 🧠 Read Together
docs.text:
Tips for 🚀 Chapter Champions (ages 9–12). Reading together for just 15 minutes a day builds vocabulary, focus and a lifelong love of stories.

Before watchingWhile watchingAfter watchingTalk about it
  • Plan the reading: watch one chapter per day and keep a short reading journal.
  • Talk about the setting — when and where does this story happen?
  • Track characters on a sticky note as they appear.
  • Notice the author’s word choices: which sentence painted the clearest picture?
  • Discuss the theme: what lesson might the author want readers to learn?
  • Try reading the next chapter on paper before watching it here.
  • Who was your favorite character in Because of Winn-Dixie, and why?
  • What was the problem in the story? How did it get solved?
  • If you could change the ending, what would happen instead?
  • How do you think the main character felt at the end?

docs.text:
Snoopy, Woodstock, and the rest of the Beagle Scouts are going on a photo hike to Point Lobos. But Point Lobos is far away, and the hike involves treacherous tall grass and maybe even queen snakes! Good grief. At least Harriet packed the angel food cake with seven-minute frosting!

docs.title: 🧠 Read Together

docs.title: 🧠 Read Together
docs.text:
Tips for 🧸 Picture Book Pals (ages 3–5). Reading together for just 15 minutes a day builds vocabulary, focus and a lifelong love of stories.

Before watchingWhile watchingAfter watchingTalk about it
  • Look at the cover together and ask: “What do you think this story is about?”
  • Turn on captions (CC) so your child sees the words while hearing them.
  • Pause and ask “What do you think will happen next?” There are no wrong answers!
  • Hunt for letters: can your child spot the first letter of their name on screen?
  • Ask your child to retell the story in three parts: beginning, middle, end.
  • Draw a favorite picture from the story and label it together.
  • Can you find your favorite picture?
  • What sounds did you hear in the story?
  • What colors did you see?

Before watchingWhile watchingAfter watchingTalk about it
  • Set a purpose: “Let’s find out why the character makes the choice they make.”

  • Jot down one new word to look up together afterwards.
  • Pause at a turning point and predict what happens next — then check!
  • Compare this story to another book you have read. What is the same? What is different?
  • Write two sentences: one thing you liked and one question you still have.

Tips for 🍼 Little Listeners (ages 0–3). Reading together for just 15 minutes a day builds vocabulary, focus and a lifelong love of stories.

Before watchingWhile watchingAfter watchingTalk about it
  • Snuggle up somewhere cozy. Your voice and your lap matter more than the screen.

  • Turn on captions (CC). Reading along with spoken words is one of the best ways to build fluency.

  • Pause the video and let your child read the next line before the narrator does.
  • Point out sight words (the, and, said, was) each time they appear.
  • Ask: “Who was the main character? What problem did they have? How was it solved?”
  • Have your child read one page aloud to you — or to a pet or stuffed animal audience!
  • Who was your favorite character in Thumbsy, The Santa Claus Sprite Who Did Nothing Quite Right, and why?
  • What was the problem in the story? How did it get solved?

docs.title: 📖 About the Book
docs.text: Sam-I-am tries to persuade the character in the top hat to try green eggs and ham. “Do you like green eggs and ham?” asks Sam-I-am in this Beginner Book by Dr. Seuss. In a house or with a mouse? In a boat or with a goat? On a train or in a tree? Sam keeps asking persistently. With unmistakable characters and signature rhymes, Dr. Seuss’s beloved favorite has cemented its place as a children’s classic. In this most famous of cumulative tales, the list of places to enjoy green eggs and ham, and friends to enjoy them with, gets longer and longer. Follow Sam-I-am as he insists that this unusual treat is indeed a delectable snack to be savored everywhere and in every way.

Tips for 🍼 Little Listeners (ages 0–3). Reading together for just 15 minutes a day builds vocabulary, focus and a lifelong love of stories.

Before watchingWhile watchingAfter watchingTalk about it
  • Snuggle up somewhere cozy. Your voice and your lap matter more than the screen.
  • Point to the cover and name what you see: “Look, a bear! What does a bear say?”
  • Pause on a page and point at pictures together. Name colors, animals and faces.
  • Copy the sounds in the story — moos, splashes, knocks. Babies learn language from your rhythm.
  • Re-read favorites. Repetition is how little brains learn words.
  • Act out one part of the story with a toy or stuffed animal.
  • Can you find your favorite picture?

  • Pause the video and let your child read the next line before the narrator does.
  • Point out sight words (the, and, said, was) each time they appear.

  • Have your child read one page aloud to you — or to a pet or stuffed animal audience!

docs.title: 📖 About the Book
docs.text: A never-before-seen picture book by Dr. Seuss! This never-ever-before-seen picture book by Dr. Seuss about making up one's mind is the literary equivalent of buried treasure! What happens when a brother and sister visit a pet store to pick a pet? Naturally, they can't choose just one! The tale captures a classic childhood moment -- choosing a pet -- and uses it to illuminate a life lesson: that it is hard to make up your mind, but sometimes you just have to do it! Told in Dr. Seuss's signature rhyming style, this is a must-have for Seuss fans and book collectors, and a perfect choice for the holidays, birthdays, and happy occasions of all kinds. An Editor's Note at the end discusses Dr. Seuss's pets, his creative process, and the discovery of the manuscript and illustrations for What Pet Should I Get? - Publisher.

docs.title: 🧠 Read Together
docs.text:
Tips for 🧸 Picture Book Pals (ages 3–5). Reading together for just 15 minutes a day builds vocabulary, focus and a lifelong love of stories.

Before watchingWhile watchingAfter watchingTalk about it
  • Look at the cover together and ask: “What do you think this story is about?”
  • Turn on captions (CC) so your child sees the words while hearing them.
  • Pause and ask “What do you think will happen next?” There are no wrong answers!
  • Hunt for letters: can your child spot the first letter of their name on screen?
  • Ask your child to retell the story in three parts: beginning, middle, end.
  • Draw a favorite picture from the story and label it together.
  • Can you find your favorite picture?
  • What sounds did you hear in the story?
  • What colors did you see?

docs.title: 🧠 Read Together
docs.text:
Reading together for just 15 minutes a day builds vocabulary, focus and a lifelong love of stories.

Before watchingWhile watchingAfter watchingTalk about it
  • Turn on captions (CC). Reading along with spoken words is one of the best ways to build fluency.
  • Read the title out loud together and talk about what you expect.
  • Pause the video and let your child read the next line before the narrator does.
  • Point out sight words (the, and, said, was) each time they appear.
  • Ask: “Who was the main character? What problem did they have? How was it solved?”
  • Have your child read one page aloud to you — or to a pet or stuffed animal audience!
  • Who was your favorite character in The Berenstain Bears' Really Big Pet Show, and why?
  • What was the problem in the story? How did it get solved?
  • If you could change the ending, what would happen instead?
  • How do you think the main character felt at the end?

docs.title: Parents' Corner
docs.text: Thank you for reading with your child! This library exists so that every kid gets story time, even on the days when grown-ups are stretched thin. Here's how to get the most out of it.

docs.title: 📺 Turn screen time into reading time
docs.text:
Switch on captions (CC)

Watching with same-language captions means your child sees each word at the moment they hear it. Researchers have found that this simple switch measurably improves reading skills, and it costs nothing. Look for the 💬 chip on a book's page: it means captions are available.

  • Sit together when you can. Even five minutes of shared reading beats an hour of solo viewing.
  • Use the pause button. Stop to ask "what do you think happens next?" Prediction builds comprehension.
  • Let them lead. Re-watching a favorite twenty times is how kids master words. It isn't wasted time!
  • Keep a routine. A story before bed or after school turns reading into a habit.

docs.title: 📚 Choosing the right book
docs.text:
Our shelves are grouped by age, but every child is different:

  • 🍼 Little Listeners (ages 0–3, Baby–Toddler)
  • 🧸 Picture Book Pals (ages 3–5, Pre-K)
  • 🌱 Early Readers (ages 5–7, K–2)
  • 🌻 Growing Readers (ages 7–9, Grades 2–4)
  • 🚀 Chapter Champions (ages 9–12, Grades 4–7)

A good rule of thumb: a book is "just right" for independent reading if your child stumbles on no more than five words on a page. Read-alongs are different. Because the narrator carries the story, kids can enjoy books a level or two above where they read on their own, and that's where a lot of vocabulary growth happens.

docs.title: 🏛️ Your library card is a superpower
docs.text: Nearly every book here can be borrowed free from a public library, in print or as an e-book or audiobook through Libby. Holding the real book while the video plays is a wonderful way to practice following along with a finger under each word.
